description: A regional copy of the Italian Dressel 1B: tall upright rim above a cylindrical neck, ovoid body ending in a solid spike, and rounded handles bearing a marked vertical groove; rims or spikes frequently carry stamps of two or three (or more) letters. Made in a hard, rough dark red to reddish-brown fabric with large white quartz/feldspar inclusions, granite fragments and golden mica, or a softer creamy-white variant.
origin: Catalan coast of northeastern Spain, especially the Barcelona region; possibly also Aspiran in southern France

description: Wide-mouthed amphora with a single (occasionally double) rounded rim above a deep groove; oval-section handles, broad neck, cylindrical body and a solid spike toe. Fabric is hard, somewhat rough and sandy with dark and white inclusions, light buff in colour; petrology shows augite, potash felspar, volcanic rock and limestone consistent with a central Italian source.

Cylindrical-bodied amphora with a thickish beaded rim and ovoid handles bearing a shallow central groove; tapers to a long hollow spike. Fabric is hard, rough and sandy with limestone and schist inclusions, dark buff in colour.

Amphora with an everted rim above a short hourglass-form neck, ovoid handles bearing a narrow central groove, and a long cylindrical body ending in a long hollow spike. Made in a hard, rough sandy light-red fabric with frequent quartz, some mica and a little felspar.
origin: Lusitania (kilns at Herdade do Pinheiro/Marateca and São Bartolomeu de Castro-Marim)

description: Cylindrical neck topped by a thickened, plain rim; round-sectioned handles run from just under the rim down to the shoulder; oval body ending in a knobbed base. Handles frequently bear stamps (Latin, sometimes Greek). Fabric is fairly hard and slightly rough, reddish-yellow to buff, with sparse white limestone inclusions plus quartz and mica.

Elongated amphora with long bifid handles made of two rods (prone to splitting into fragments), a simple rounded rim, a marked carination at the shoulder, and a solid, slightly flared spike base. Body walls thinner than Dressel 1; often stamped near the spike (also on neck or handle) with two or three letters.
origin: Western Mediterranean: Campania, Latium and Etruria (Italy), Catalonia and Baetica (Spain), and southern/central France; based on Aegean (Kos) prototypes

description: Spanish fish-sauce amphora with two varieties: (A) a flaring bell-shaped mouth with a thickened short rim concave on the outside, a stout cylindrical neck, long flattened handles bent sharply just under the rim, and a bulbous 'radish-shaped' body ending in a long hollow spike; (B) similar but with a less flaring rim. Cadiz fabric is hard, slightly rough and sandy, reddish-buff with sparse red iron-ore inclusions, often with an off-white slip.
origin: Southern Spanish coast (Form B possibly Catalonia)

description: A group of typologically related ovoid amphorae sharing a rounded ovoid body and a central furrow/groove down the handles. Five rim and spike variants (A–E) are distinguished. Fabrics are generally soft, fine and light buff in colour.
origin: Southern Spain (kilns at Algeciras, Cerro de los Mártires, Puerto Real); possibly also Catalonia/Mediterranean

description: Tall amphora with a short everted rim above a long slender neck, ovoid (loop) handles, a cylindrical body and a short solid spike base. Fabric is soft, powdery and sandy with occasional white inclusions, typically reddish-buff.
origin: Southern Spanish coast, made at Algeciras (El Rinconcillo)

description: Amphora with an everted collar rim and oval handles bearing a fairly deep vertical groove; cylindrical body ending in a solid conical spike. Rarely stamped. Hard rough buff fabric similar to Dressel 20 but body walls noticeably thinner with tighter curvature.
A wide neck with a hooked rim and long flattened recurved handles; the body broadens toward the base and finishes in a long hollow spike. Likely a later development of Class 17.
origin: Southern Spanish coast (Cadiz region a major production centre)

description: Greco-Italic amphora with a triangular rim, cylindrical neck and carinated shoulder. Ovoid handles run from just below the rim to the shoulders, occasionally bearing Greek, Latin or Iberian stamps. Body typically pear-shaped ending in a short solid spike. Five forms (a-e) recognised by Will (1982); Form d illustrated. Distinctive volcanic fabric (Form a2) is buff with pyroxene, quartz, potash feldspar, mica and volcanic rock fragments.
origin: Italy (Sicily, near Cosa and Pompeii), with Aegean and Spanish forms; Form d probably near Cosa and Pompeii

description: Thick, almost vertical collar-rim (frequently stamped) over a heavy cylindrical body. Long oval rod-like handles and a solid chunky spike that tends to splay slightly at the tip. Stamps usually on the rim (occasionally the neck), typically two or three letters. Fabric matches that of Dressel 1A.
origin: Italy — chiefly Campania, Latium and Etruria

description: Narrow neck with a projecting triangular rim; two broad handles bent sharply round, each with a single central groove. High-shouldered pear-shaped (piriform) body ending in a short spike. Hard, rough sandy fabric, light reddish-brown, with abundant quartz, muscovite flecks and some potash feldspar.
origin: Uncertain; possibly Spain, with similar piriform vessels common in Portugal

description: Tall amphora with a fairly heavy projecting rim and two thick rounded handles running from rim to shoulder; long cylindrical body that swells slightly near the base before tapering to a short spike. Fabric is hard, rough and sandy with small white limestone inclusions, buff in colour.
origin: Uncertain — variously argued for Spain, the Algarve of Portugal, or North Africa

description: Large globular-bodied transport amphora with thick, sharply angled or oval-sectioned handles, a short neck often with an inward-curving (concave) rim, and a small basal knob. Developed from the Augustan prototype (Class 24); rim evolution is well charted. Frequently bears a relief stamp in a rectangular frame near the top of the handle. Thick, rough sandy fabric (buff, light reddish-brown or grey) with prominent quartz and feldspar inclusions reflecting Guadalquivir geology.
origin: Baetica, southern Spain (Guadalquivir valley between Seville and Cordoba, Andalusia)

description: Related to Classes 27 and 28: a thickened rim above a neck marked by two outer step-like inflections, short flat handles with a central groove, broad rounded shoulders, a thin-walled tapering body, and a narrow flat base with a small footring.
origin: Southern France (kilns at Corneilhan and Velaux; a related form at Marseilles)

description: Two related Tripolitanian forms. Variant A (Tripolitanian II) has a thickened everted rim with a sharp groove on its outer face, a short upright neck, two short handles set below the shoulder, and a long cylindrical body. Variant B (Tripolitanian III) has an everted collar rim with a short neck; from the 2nd century AD a clay plug is often set inside the spike. Occasionally stamped on rim and handle.

Thick rounded rim with short flat grooved handles set crudely on a short neck; broad rounded shoulders pass into a thin-walled tapering body, often slightly corrugated on the upper part and showing trimming below. Narrow flat base carries a small footring. Hard, faintly micaceous cream to creamy-pink fabric with quartz, mica and limestone inclusions.
origin: Southern France, chiefly around the mouth of the Rhône in Languedoc, with kilns also at Crouzilles (Indre-et-Loire)

description: Cylindrical transport amphora with a thickened, fairly upright or slightly rounded rim, short upright neck and small sharply bent handles. Long cylindrical body ending in a short spike, sometimes with a slight bulge. Panella divided it into four sub-types: IIA (cylindrical neck, rounder handles), IIB/IIC (conical neck, narrower body, less rounded handles), and IID (vertical rim thickened internally, a late third/fourth-century variant). Occasionally neck-stamped with place-name initials or a tria nomina.
origin: Sahel region of central Tunisia (Roman Byzacena)
contents: olive oil, possibly also fish products

description: Narrow-necked amphora with a carinated shoulder, rounded handles sometimes bearing shallow vertical fluting, and a squat body on a footed base. Two rim variants: a sharply biconical rim (form A, common in the western Mediterranean, becoming less sharp by the 4th c.) and a thickened, slightly inturned rim (form B). Hard, fairly smooth pale red to pale brown fabric with small limestone inclusions, quartz, foraminifera, plagioclase felspar and mica flecks.

Narrow-necked amphora with bowed handles running from mid-neck to shoulder, a cylindrical body, and a rounded base ending in a small point. Two rim variants noted: one with a slight ridge at the rim/neck junction and a gently convex rim, the other flatter and ridgeless (later, third-century). Typically hard, smooth buff fabric with white limestone inclusions and mica.
origin: Keratokambos kiln in southern Crete, with other production likely on mainland Greece

description: Tall cylindrical-bodied amphora with two small side handles and a flaring rim. Van der Werff divided it into three sub-forms: Form 1 with a widely flaring rim thickened below and sometimes a flange on the outer face; Form 2 similar but simpler, smaller and with a hollow spike; Form 3 with an everted rim of near-vertical outer face and a less pronounced hollow spike. North African fabric range with frequent wind-rounded quartz grains and limestone.
origin: North Africa: kiln at Kouass (Morocco) and the Carthage region for Form 1, Tunisia for Form 2, Tripolitania for Form 3; widely distributed in the western Mediterranean

description: Likely precursor to Dressel 20, but with an ovoid body, slimmer handles and a fairly developed spike. Rim is rounded, occasionally with an internal hollow. Fabric matches Dressel 20.
origin: Guadalquivir valley between Seville and Cordoba, Baetica (southern Spain)

description: Amphora with a thickened rim, often bevelled on its inner edge, a bulging neck, arched bifid handles and an ovoid body tapering to a short basal knob. Fabric is hard and fairly smooth with small white limestone inclusions (and some foraminifera, quartz, epidote and mica flecks), light brown to buff in colour. Handle treatment resembles that of Class 10.

Flat-based amphora related to Class 27: short flat handles with a central groove, broad rounded shoulders, thin-walled tapering body to a flat base with a small footring, and a characteristic broad, thick flat rim.

A tall-necked amphora with a plain rounded rim and flattish handles bearing a shallow central groove; the base is flat with a narrow footring. Fabric is a hard, fairly smooth sandy ware, creamish-grey, with small white limestone inclusions plus quartz and flecks of mica.

Vertical rim (occasionally ribbed) above a short neck, with sharply angled handles that may be ribbed, a pear-shaped tapering body, and a small hollow bulbous base. Handles sometimes carry stamps indicating origin. Fabric is hard grey-buff with conspicuous angular white inclusions and an off-white exterior slip.

Tall amphora with a thickened rim that is concave on its outer face, atop a fairly tall slightly conical neck. Short, thickish handles lead to a long cylindrical body ending in a hollow conical spike. Occasionally stamped on rim and handle. Two fabrics: a finer pinkish-red one with rough white-skinned surfaces and a coarser hard brick-red one with limestone inclusions.

Resembles a late Dressel 20 but smaller in scale: a short triangular rim, two small oval handles that loop sharply just below it, a rounded bulbous body and a short spike base. Stamps occasionally appear near the top of the handle.
origin: Same source area as Class 25 (Baetica, southern Spain); evolved from Dressel 20

description: Globular-bodied amphora with a short conical neck, tall everted rim, and curved handles running from shoulder to neck. The upper body bears closely-set deep horizontal grooves (straight or wavy) and the base ends in a small knob. Hard, fine fabric, buff to light red, with visible white limestone inclusions and a little mica.
origin: Uncertain; concentration in the Aegean and Black Sea region suggests an eastern source, possibly near Kounoupi in the Argolid
contents: Not known (resin in some Roumanian finds may reflect reuse)

description: Cylindrical amphora with a thickened everted rim (convex outside, concave inside), short straight neck and small sharply bent handles; long cylindrical body ending in a short hollow spike. Neck sometimes stamped with place-name initials or a tria nomina. Central Tunisian fabric is hard, brick-red with a black outer zone and often a white saline skin smoothed in vertical brush strokes; subangular quartz with limestone inclusions.
origin: Sahel region of central Tunisia (Roman Byzacena); a related form made at Ariana near Carthage
contents: fish products, possibly also olive oil

description: Amphora with a distinctive 'pulley-wheel' rim and short rounded handles bearing one or two shallow grooves; a well-rounded body terminates in a thick, broad footring. Resembles Class 27 but distinguished by its characteristic rim and heavier footring; sometimes stamped on the neck. Fabric soft and slightly rough, fine-textured, pinkish-buff, with quartz, mica and limestone inclusions.
origin: Tarraconensis, possibly Baetica (Spain), and France (kiln at Velaux, Bouches-du-Rhône)
contents: Uncertain; possibly wine (French vessels) and wine or fish products (Spanish vessels)

description: Amphora with a fairly thick, gently convex flared collar rim and short flat handles bearing two grooves; bulbous body on a broad flat base with a small footring. Neck stamps occur occasionally.
origin: Southern France (Provence at Velaux; Languedoc at Eyrieux, Marcoule, Four and Boyas)

description: Ovoid amphora with relatively thin walls and widely spaced ridging across the mid-body, tapering toward shoulder and base. Thick stubby handles and a thickened rim with a slightly concave outer face; red dipinti in Greek cursive often on the shoulder. Hard sandy fabric with limestone inclusions, pinkish-cream to reddish-yellow. Both a larger (A) and smaller (B) version exist.
origin: Eastern Mediterranean, probably the Antioch region of northern Syria

description: Late Roman cylindrical North African amphorae in a wide variety of forms, distinguished mainly by differences in rim and spike profiles; long tubular bodies ending in solid or hollow spikes, with short handles at the neck.

Bag-shaped amphora with a vertical rim springing directly from the shoulder (no neck) and a body widening to a rounded base; two ring handles set on the shoulder. Surface usually corrugated and bears white painted decoration. Fabric in two versions: a soft, very sandy reddish-orange and a hard, thin grey often with a reddish core.

Small globular amphora with a flat base, narrow neck and a thick rim bearing several grooves on its upper surface; handles also commonly furrowed. Fabric is hard, smooth and finely sandy, reddish-yellow throughout, with abundant well-sorted fine quartz and rare cryptocrystalline limestone.

Narrow cylindrical-bodied amphora with a small everted rim and rough loop handles set on the shoulder, ending in a rounded or occasionally flat base. Marked ridging on the shoulder and between handles, with lumps of clay applied to shoulder and rim before firing. Hard, sandy drab-brown fabric with scattered white limestone and abundant well-sorted angular quartz.
contents: Gaza wine (possibly olive oil or sesame oil)

description: Amphora with a conical neck and everted, thickened rim; thick, slightly bowed oval handles running from the upper neck to the shoulder and rising to rim level; a bag-shaped body ending in a rounded base. Fabric variants include a medium-hard orange ware and a hard sandy-grey ware fired reddish at the margins with small white inclusions, rich in limestone (with foraminifera) and quartz.

Slender amphora with an elongated narrow body, a long tapering spike, and a relatively tall neck ending in an everted rim with two short handles attached to the neck. Both a larger and smaller variant are known. Hard, rough, sandy fabric ranging from light red to light buff, frequently with a greenish-cream slip; quartz and often limestone inclusions.
origin: Cartagena (Spain) and probably North Africa; likely made in several places

description: Short neck with an upright rim above a sharply carinated shoulder; long tapering body ending in a solid spike. Thick ridging on shoulder and body; later (6th–7th c.) examples have taller necks and more conical shoulders. A variant shows a short neck with two small handles from shoulder-top to rim and screw-like corrugations on the spike. Soft, rough sandy micaceous brown fabric with frequent subangular quartz and occasional chaff/grass voids.

Slender amphora with a long narrow neck, two short strap-handles, high rounded shoulders and a solid tapering foot; broad shallow ribbing covers most of the body. An earlier single-handled variant with an open hollow foot also exists. Fabric is hard, fairly thin-walled, smooth and strongly micaceous, deep reddish-brown.
origin: Eastern Mediterranean, probably western Asia Minor

description: Tall amphora with a long cylindrical grooved neck and two short handles running from rim to upper neck; the body is long, narrow and slightly tapering, ending in a small knobbed base. Made of distinctive Nile clay.

Small thickened rim with two ring handles set on the shoulder above a heavy bag-shaped body that tapers to a rounded base; coarse heavy ridging often appears between the handles and on the base. Hard, fairly rough fabric with scattered white limestone inclusions, dark buff surface over a brown core with a light red zone.
origin: Probably Palestine (possibly Gaza); likely a precursor of Class 49

description: Small amphora with a slender spindle-shaped body tapering to a point, fitted with handles made of a single oval-sectioned rod of clay. Fabric is hard and reddish-buff with a creamy outer surface, containing abundant rounded limestone inclusions up to 3 mm.

Thick broad handles steeply arched above a narrow rim, with a prominent sharpish flange beneath; tall thick conical neck, tapering body, and a tubular hollowed base bearing shallow horizontal grooves. Fabric is hard, rough orange-red with frequent quartz inclusions and ferruginous sandstone fragments.
Plate/dish with a weakly curved oblique wall ending in a rounded bead-rim, often accompanied by an interior groove; tall steep ring foot.
Subtype distinguished from 3.1 by greater depth and a straighter oblique wall; rounded distinct lip and tall ring foot.
Very steep, stiff version with a barely emphasized lip and a low foot.
Bowl with a sharp carination between flaring wall and floor; strongly profiled, pronounced hanging lip with no interior articulation.
Carinated bowl with flaring wall; vertical hanging lip whose upper rim zone is set off by a groove.
Carinated bowl with steeper wall; shorter hanging lip that is profiled on the interior.
Transitional plate: exterior profile like Subform 18.2 but with a pronounced convex moulding at the base of the wall on the interior, similar to 19.2.
Plate with rim mouldings as Subform 18.2 and a quarter-round moulding between rim and floor; the most common variant of the form.

Plate with rim mouldings as Subform 18.2 but with a flat step (usually rouletted) between rim and floor; a rare variant, with example 19.3.2 bearing four applied motifs on the step instead of rouletting.

Hemispherical cup with S-shaped profile and a wide rim that droops/curves downward; usually decorated with two grape clusters and lilies in barbotine; varying foot-ring heights with flat or center-thickened base. The most common subform.
Variant with a small ledge/listel at the inner junction of the rim, recalling mortaria; otherwise the hemispherical drooping-rim profile of 43.1.
Variant with a flattened rim curvature, approaching the profile of Form 44; barbotine decoration at the rim.

Conical cup with concave vertical rim; external and internal rim mouldings as Subform 18.2, rim rises from wall at an angle without overhang, convex mouldings above and below usually rouletted; occasional applied double spirals.
origin: principal centres of TS production (few from Arezzo); largest examples from Ateius workshops at Pisa

description: Like 22.1 but rim axis slopes outward, more or less continuing the wall line; associated with slightly convex body, curved floor and externally grooved foot; sometimes a narrow band of rouletting low on the wall. Exclusive to Puteoli.
Central rim element flat (not concave) on outer face; lower convex moulding projects downward forming a marked overhang where it meets the wall. Produced only by T. Mallius Fortunatus at Lyon.
Rim as 22.1 but compressed and inclined inward.
Outer face of rim as 22.1, inner face a single convex element set off at the lip and at the body junction by grooves; occasional applied double spirals.
Like 22.5 but with all details reduced to a minimum; simpler, coarser execution typical of Padana factories, without applied decoration.

Cylindrical cup with flat floor and straight vertical wall; a moulding at the base of the wall acts as a low ring-foot; rim thickened or everted. Mid-height usually carries a band of convex mouldings or grooves, occasionally plain.
origin: North and central Italy (incl. Tardo-Italica and Tardo-Padana)

description: Cylindrical cup with flat floor, vertical slightly concave wall and plain rim; two vertical ring-handles set on the wall, resting on an oblique ring-foot.
Open form with a flat, outward-flaring upper wall; rouletted (guilloché) body bounded by grooves, plain rim, and a pair of vertical ring-handles with eyelet-like support plate.
Hemispherical rounded-wall cup with rouletted exterior bounded by grooves; vertical ring-handles with eyelet support plate; low ring foot. Sometimes stamped (here LAVRI).
Hemispherical cup variant with strongly incurved rim; rouletted lower body, vertical ring-handles, and a low ring foot.

Dish with an S-shaped profile and curving (convex) wall; the wall may be articulated by ridges or grooves. Wide, outward-flaring rim that droops downward, decorated in barbotine with grape clusters and lilies. Low ring foot. Unstamped.

Bowl with a gently curved sloping wall passing into a rounded floor; rim variously formed, either slightly everted or as a beaded lip; low slanted ring foot, sometimes grooved, with interior grooves on the floor.
origin: Arezzo; Padana B/C; also local ware of Bram/Narbonne

description: Variant with a stiffer, straighter sloping wall, occasional grooving inside; the rim is variously thickened. Affinity to Forms 13 and 14.
Like 8.2 but with a sharp angular break (carination) between floor and sloping wall; variously thickened rim.
Footless cup with a steep, lightly curved wall meeting the flat base in an external edge; underside slightly convex, with concentric grooves on the inner floor of good examples.
Plain upright rim with a quarter-round moulding at the rim/floor junction; merges with the curved-rim subform 6.2.
Rim moulded as in subform 20.3 with a quarter-round moulding below at the rim/floor transition.
Rim moulded as in subform 20.4 with a quarter-round moulding beneath; the Padana variant (21.3.2) shows plainer execution and an outward-sloping rim.
Rim moulded as in subform 20.5 with a quarter-round moulding at the rim/floor junction.
Plain upright rim with a flat step (often rouletted on top) between rim and floor; compare subform 6.4.
Rim moulded as in subform 20.3 with a flat (usually rouletted) step beneath.
Rim moulded as in subform 20.4 with a flat (usually rouletted) step beneath.
Rim moulded as in subform 20.5 with a flat (usually rouletted) step at the rim/floor junction.
Bell-shaped cup with a close-set hanging lip; inner wall shows a convex-then-concave curve. Standring upright, usually a groove on the outer wall.
origin: Etruria and Lyon, rarely the Po valley

description: Bell-shaped cup whose interior is tripartite: a hollow groove plus a wider or narrower bulge with concave sweep toward the base; close-set hanging lip.
origin: Etruria and Lyon, rarely the Po valley

description: Bell-shaped cup with an unarticulated inner wall; only the lip is set off, otherwise a smooth steep profile.
origin: Etruria and Lyon, rarely the Po valley

description: Bell-shaped cup with a merely rudimentary lip that may disappear entirely; otherwise plain steep wall on a low foot.
origin: Etruria and Lyon, rarely the Po valley

description: Cup with conical to slightly curving wall set on a chamfered ring-foot; upper part of the body richly profiled with several mouldings near the rim, a more elaborate version of the Form 22 rim.
Plate with triangular-sectioned hanging lip close to the wall; interior rim and inner wall articulated with a bead and groove, wall inclination varying. Corresponds to Service Ib.
Plate with hanging lip; inner wall gently convex with little or no profiling. Corresponds to Service Ib.
Plate with inner wall divided in three (groove–bead–groove); exterior wall-to-floor transition rounded. Corresponds to Service Ic.
Plate with tripartite inner wall (groove–bead–groove); exterior wall-to-floor transition with an angular break. Corresponds to Service Ic.
Like 12.4 but with a two-stepped interior profile, usually featuring two grooves, occasionally a single groove and curvature. Corresponds to Service Ic.

Dish with curving, upswept wall set off from a flat floor by ridges inside and out; broad horizontal rim with an inner ridge, two grooves and barbotine decoration (grape clusters and lilies). Low wide ring foot.

Platter/plate with sloping wall and a vertical, slightly concave rim; body, foot and inner rim profile follow Form 12, with the outer rim sometimes framed above and below by narrow convex mouldings as on Forms 18-19.
Campanulate cup with chamfered ring-foot and a concave vertical rim; rolled (rouletted) convex mouldings top and bottom of rim, the inner rim face divided in two as on Subforms 18.2/22.1.
Campanulate cup variant with a broad concave moulding on the inner rim face, set off from the body and at the lip by grooves; chamfered ring-foot and rouletted rim mouldings.
Degenerate campanulate cup with a flatter outer rim face and smooth straight inner face meeting the body at a sharp angle (as Subform 23.2), set on a low foot.
Plate with a widely flaring curved wall passing smoothly into a flat floor; simple rim.
Plate whose floor rises toward the wall in a gentle continuous curve; plain rim.
Plate with a flat floor and a small step/offset at the junction with the rising wall.
Plate with a steep wall, the lip sometimes set off by grooves; the variant 4.4.2 has a very low wall.
Plate with an incurving wall and a bipartite (two-stage) interior profile; flaring foot.
Thin-walled plate with a steep, upswept wall and tall steep foot; lip may be marked by grooves, often with simple applied ornament.
Like 4.6 but the wall is framed outside by a rib above and below (sometimes ribbed); the lower rib may project strongly.
Early variant of the vertical-rimmed platter; shows only some of the developed features, with a flat floor and a concave vertical rim not yet fully formed.

Standard developed version: vertical concave rim with clearly defined convex external mouldings (often rouletted) and a carefully bipartite internal moulding; flat floor with grooves and central stamp, oblique ring-foot.
As the standard version but with the uppermost element of the rim grossly enlarged relative to the lower parts; some overlap with Form 6.1.

Platter/plate with straight oblique wall and plain rounded or pointed rim; floor flat or slightly dished, usually bearing a grooved (rouletted) band; broad or narrow ring foot set obliquely, sometimes grooved on the exterior, occasionally with a small interior step.
origin: Arezzo, Po valley (Padana), with local imitations in South Gaul and Campania

description: Subform with a low upright rim and variable interior profiling; rare, occurring only in red ware with a flat floor; gradual transitions toward Form 18.1.
origin: Arezzo, Po valley (Padana), with local imitations in South Gaul and Campania

description: Bell-shaped cup with an outward-bulging rim taller than Form 14; inner wall profile reads concave-convex-concave, usually emphasized by grooves (occasionally without). Triangular-sectioned ring foot, grooves on outer wall.
origin: Etruria, possibly Campania, and Lyon (local Gallic workshops, Saint-Romain-en-Gal)

description: Bell-shaped cup whose inner wall is articulated into three slightly concave segments; rim finished with a rounded bead lip. Triangular-sectioned ring foot.
origin: Etruria, possibly Campania, and Lyon (local Gallic workshops, Saint-Romain-en-Gal)

description: Conical cup with plain tapering rim leaning slightly inward; flat or biconical floor meeting wall at sharp interior angle, on a low foot; sometimes with applied decoration.
Conical cup with a flat-faced outer rim carrying applied decoration framed above and below by convex mouldings; inner rim face plain or with a groove at the lip; flat foot.

Straight to gently curved sloping wall passing in a rounded transition into a flat floor; rim and wall usually plain but sometimes with grooves or small steps inside/outside; proportions of height to rim diameter vary; base formed as in Form 14.
Small bowl whose steep, straight sloping wall meets the flat floor at a sharp angle (knick); low foot ring, sometimes grooved/profiled.

Hemispherical cup; the earlier wall-rib of Form 33 replaced by a roughly horizontal projecting flange, above which a short steep rim rises (vertical or sloping inward), usually carrying applied spiral ornament; rim set off by grooves, narrow tall foot tapering downward.
Variant of the same flanged form but with an overall flatter, wide-spreading body; horizontal wall flange with steep applique-decorated rim above, narrow high foot.
Round-walled cup with an encircling rib and rouletting/grooving above it like Form 33, but distinguished by a horizontally projecting offset lip.
Conical cup with an upright convex rim that curves inward, set off from the wall by a fine groove; grooving at the lip inside/outside, decorated with rouletting and/or applied motifs.
Conical cup similar to 24.1 but with the rim offset from the wall line forming a marked overhang; bears applied decoration.
Conical cup with rim divided from the wall by a narrow pronounced convex moulding; curving floor and heavy stepped foot, without applied decoration. Distinctive Padana subform.
Small shallow cup with a convex rim turned in sharply from the wall; rim may carry rouletting and applied spirals.

Carinated cup: shallow conical lower part set off from a flat floor, steep straight wall with vertical plain rim marked off by a groove; low ring-foot. Often applied double spirals below lip and grooves/rouletting at carination.
Like subform 26.1 but the wall bears an additional triple convex moulding on the outside, sometimes echoed by concave mouldings inside; carinated profile on low ring-foot.
Pronounced overhang at the carination with slightly concave wall; shallower lower body than 26.1, curving smoothly into the floor; foot generally heavy. Rare.
Like 26.3 (overhang at carination, heavy foot) but with a straighter wall and decorated with a triple moulding as on subform 26.2.
Platter/plate with curving wall and a trough-like, channelled rim divided into three parts by two grooves; flat or gently rising floor on a low footring.
Plate with curving wall and a simply rounded, offset lip; low footring, floor flat to gently rising.
Plate whose lip is drawn forward/outward and slightly grooved on top; in Padana C variants a minimal footring set far out near the wall edge.
Plate with a lip pulled straight out and flattened on top; broad shallow form with low footring and a slight inner step on the floor.
Hemispherical cup with a flat horizontal rim; sharp, ridge-marked transition from wall to rim. Walls may carry grooves and barbotine ornament; sits on an angular/triangular-section ring foot.
Hemispherical cup with a flat horizontal rim, but the wall-to-rim junction is rounded and unemphasized, recalling Form 43; low ring foot.

Hemispherical cup with a continuous external rib on the wall; rim is incurved and set fairly high, lip offset by a groove, upper wall usually rouletted/grooved and often decorated with two applied spirals; low ring foot.
More open hemispherical cup than 33.1 with the wall rib set lower; rouletted upper wall, low ring foot.
Very shallow, widely flaring version of the form with strongly out-turned wall carrying the rib; low foot. Dated later (late 1st–early 2nd c. AD on stamp evidence).
Rare variant with very steep, almost vertical wall and a relatively low rim compared to overall height; rib on wall, rouletted band, low foot.
Transitional form between 33.4 and Form 26 (26.3): rounded, up-turned floor but with a steep, straight upper wall carrying the rib; low foot.
Carinated cylindrical cup with small flat lip; straight wall sloping slightly outward, smooth, with flat floor sharply set off from a conical lower body; ring foot.
As 27.1 but with a triple convex moulding on the exterior at mid-height; flat lip, straight outward-sloping wall, ring foot.
Smooth wall sloping markedly outward, with the lower body curving smoothly into the floor; flat lip; rare variant.

Arretine cup with finely profiled constriction and a rounded, outward-curving rim; overall shape can be steeper or more flaring; top of lip often grooved, sometimes with two applied spirals; rectangular-section ring foot.
Padanian cup, somewhat coarser than 32.1, rarely rilled and never with applied spirals; constricted wall with distinct rim and ring foot.
Cup as 32.1 but with a sharply set-off, horizontally projecting rim.
Cup with high-set constriction, only slightly thickened and undecorated rim, and a tall ring foot.
Cup with only faintly indicated constriction and a barely thickened, undecorated rim; low form on ring foot.
Plate with straight oblique wall meeting the floor at an angle; short, slightly outward-curved lip; low, fairly broad, externally grooved foot. No interior markings.
As 2.1 but with a three-part (tripartite) lip derived from Campana ware, comparable to the lips of Forms 5.1, 10.2 and 13.1.
Wall bent outward with only a weakly accentuated lip; both plates and dishes occur. Known so far only in Padana C ware.
Large shallow plate with a broad, far-projecting articulated rim that slopes obliquely and is strongly undercut; low wide ring foot, underside unglazed inside the ring.
Plate with broad projecting rim as in 10.1 but with an external groove/channel cut on the rim's outer face.
Plate with a shortened, upward-drawn rim that is often stunted and barely undercut; upper surface of the rim more or less profiled.

Dish with rounded up-curving wall set off by a groove; horizontal rim sharply offset by a carination, running level or slightly downward, with an upturned raised edge; low flat ring foot, sometimes barbotine-decorated wall.

Dish whose rim emerges in a smooth continuous curve from a long stretched wall (no sharp knick); raised vertical edge at rim margin; ring foot with markedly smaller radius than 41.1, barbotine motifs on wall.

Cup with rounded, upturned wall divided by a sharp horizontal constriction at about mid-height; upper wall ribbed/rouletted, lip set off by a groove, on a tall ring foot. Sub-type 31.1.1 has a steeper upper wall, 31.1.2 a more strongly everted upper wall.
Cup with a high-set constriction; ribbing/rouletting extends over the lower part of the wall as well, with offset lip and tall ring foot (Puteolan characteristics).

Hemispherical body with a sharp grooved carination separating the rounded lower wall from a slightly hollowed, drooping horizontal lip; lip surface fluted and decorated with two small spiral appliqués; low broad ring foot.
Hemispherical body whose lip projects inward as a ledge above the horizontal rim; rim top fluted and ornamented with two small spiral appliqués; low broad ring foot.
Like 37.1 but with a narrower, undecorated lip and a foot that tapers downward.
Hemispherical body with an undecorated lip that curves out smoothly from the wall; possible grooves on the body; low ring foot.
Hemispherical body with a strong, triangular thickened lip; undecorated.

Dish with oblique straight wall and broad horizontal rim; angular floor-to-wall and wall-to-rim transitions accentuated by grooves and ridges; rim flat or slightly dropped, decorated with two grooves and barbotine ornament; often stamped.
Dish with sloping wall and horizontal rim; rounded, unemphasized transitions from floor to wall and to the flat rim, lacking the grooves/ridges of 42.1; barbotine-decorated rim.

Flat plate/platter with a well-set-off, undercut rim that widens into a triangular-sectioned, pendant vertical lip ('hanging lip'). Inner rim and inner wall divided into a curve and a hollow groove, often emphasized by grooves; flat floor on Italic pieces decorated inside with grooves and rouletting; mostly radial stamping.
origin: Etruria (esp. Arezzo) and the Po Valley (Padana); local workshops in southern France

description: Wide flaring, fully smooth hemispherical cup on a broad angular ring foot; no decoration, always unstamped.
Obliquely rising, only slightly curved wall with the lip set off by grooves; foot ring with tall rectangular or triangular section.
Cup with an incurved smooth rim and a grooved/rilled band bounded by grooves running around the body at varying heights; low foot ring, edged on the outside and flat-beveled inside.
Hemispherical or flatter flaring cup, plain or with grooves at the rim and sometimes on the body, rarely with appliqué spirals; low broad foot ring.
Plate with a plain vertical rim, parallel-sided or slightly tapering toward the lip, meeting the floor at a sharp angle; slim tall foot. Some late examples carry applied decoration.
origin: Italian workshops (incl. Padana region and Late Italian potters)

description: Like 20.1 but the outer face of the vertical rim bears an extra triple moulding. Uncommon, attributable to the first half of the 1st century AD.
origin: Italian workshops (incl. Padana region and Late Italian potters)

description: Rim with doubled convex mouldings top and bottom on the exterior, usually a broad band of rouletting between them; interior groove at lip or a faint bipartite division. Applied double spirals and other motifs common.
origin: Italian workshops (incl. Padana region and Late Italian potters)

description: Rim with simple convex mouldings top and bottom outside, plain or with a groove at lip; outer face very commonly carries varied applied motifs. The most common mid-1st-century plate form.
origin: Italian workshops (incl. Padana region and Late Italian potters)

description: Like 20.4 but with an additional triple moulding on the outer face; often combined with applied decoration. Uncommon, first half of the 1st century AD.
origin: Italian workshops (incl. Padana region and Late Italian potters)

description: Small cylindrical cup with flat floor and low ring-foot; rim and lower wall plain or set off by fine grooves on the exterior, with a fine groove inside at the lip.
Cylindrical cup whose rim is formed into a convex moulding bounded by grooves and decorated with rouletting; a groove, sometimes with rouletting, also marks the base of the wall.
Cylindrical cup with a slightly flaring wall and a short flat lip, on a low ring-foot.
Plate with a tall, widely flaring upper wall rounded into the floor; surface can carry grooves and rilling. Only plates known, closely related to Form 15.
Standard plate form akin to 4.6 with a high foot, curved transition between rim and floor, often applied spiral motifs and stamps in the floor; Padana examples tend toward coarse, uneven proportions.
Basic shape like 6.2 but the wall is framed by two grooves.
Instead of a rounded transition there is a usually rilled step; wall is low and smooth and may carry appliqués.
Like 6.4 but the wall is bordered by grooves, which can be rilled or decorated with appliqués.
Tall beaker with a slightly bulbous body, disk-shaped base and a grooved lip; lower roughly two-thirds carry relief decoration, sometimes separated from the plain upper zone by a groove or step.
origin: Northern Italy (also briefly made at Lyon)

description: Bulbous cup constricted at mid-height with an incurving rim grooved at the lip, resting on a disk base or low foot and fitted with two vertical strap handles; moulded relief decoration on the lower body.
Low platter footring with a broad resting surface; outer face can be strongly concave/grooved; radially stamped (early–middle Augustan group).
Low broad platter footring, outer side hollowed; belongs to early–mid Augustan radially stamped platters.
Low platter footring with wide standing face; early–mid Augustan, radially stamped.
Low platter footring of the early–mid Augustan group, broad resting surface, outer profile can be strongly grooved.
Low platter footring with wide base, early–mid Augustan, radially stamped.
Augustan–Tiberian footring, generally taller than wide with rectangular or trapezoidal cross-section; initially radial then central stamping.
Augustan–Tiberian footring, taller than broad, rectangular/trapezoidal section, central stamp.
Augustan–Tiberian footring, narrow and tall with rectangular section; central stamping.
Augustan–Tiberian tall footring, trapezoidal/rectangular cross-section, centrally stamped.
Augustan–Tiberian footring, higher than wide, rectangular section; central stamp.
Very tall, slender footring of the Tiberian–Flavian group, central p.p. stamp.
Very high, narrow footring (Tiberian–Flavian), thin floor, central p.p. stamp.
Hemispherical chalice on a pedestal foot, distinguished by an elaborate rim with alternating convex and concave mouldings, more pronounced than the related preceding form.
Chalice with hemispherical body and tall vertical rim on a pedestal foot; rim set off from body by several exterior grooves, with grooves or a small convex moulding at the lip.

Tall-rimmed chalice with hemispherical body and pedestal foot; heavy multiple mouldings at the lip and a sharply defined, often rouletted convex moulding separating the rim from the relief-decorated body.
Tall-rimmed chalice on pedestal foot with simple projecting mouldings at the lip and at the junction between rim and body; latest variant with a reduced mould-made zone.

Chalice with hemispherical body on a pedestal foot; relief decoration on the body is capped by grooves, above which a plain flaring zone rises to a near-vertical convex rim. Rim often framed by fine grooves or cordons and usually rouletted; inner rim has a concave lip moulding over a convex one, separated by offsets.
Chalice in which the rim is a convex quarter-round element set off sharply from the body, like a lid seating, placed directly above the relief decoration; rouletting may be absent.
Chalice with a steep, near-vertical wall ending in a sharp carination above a low splaying foot; wall bears applied (appliqué) figural decoration.
Chalice-krater with an outward-flaring wall decorated in barbotine, fitted with small handles, on a low pedestal foot.
Cylindrical jar with flat base and 'split' rim; outer rim ends plain or slightly thickened, usually articulated with grooves. The perforated inner insert narrows the opening.
Cylindrical jar where the outer rim widens above the insert into a squared opening; perforated inner insert.
Small inkwell with footring, narrowed central opening and an extra small off-centre hole; wall rounded to carinated.
Small inkwell with cylindrical wall, narrowed central opening, extra small hole, and two little handles.

Conical open cup matching the Form 42 plates; horizontal or slightly drooping flat rim, body decorated with grooves and barbotine motifs (paired grapes and lilies, occasionally spirals); low ring foot below the wall junction, with a flat or gently domed floor.
Flat-floored dish with sharp basal angle and flaring concave wall ending in a short upright rim ledge clearly offset both inside and out; wall may be more incurved or shallower; low ring foot.
Flat-floored flaring dish whose rim has a triangular profile that is not offset on the interior, marked only by grooves; low ring foot.
Footring outer-edged (in early phase fluted); floor runs flat beyond the ring then turns up sharply (angular junction) into an oblique wall.
Edged footring; flat floor projecting beyond the ring with a sharp-angled rise into a shallow oblique wall (angular wall junction).
Edged footring with flat outward-extending floor and a sharp or slightly rounded angular kink into a steeper wall.
Floor flares out past the footring as in B3.1-3 but the wall transition is rounded; footring fluted in early period, later edged and higher.
Flat outward-flaring floor with a smoothly rounded junction into the wall; footring edged.
Rounded wall junction with a flaring floor, sometimes with an interior offset; edged footring.
Base rounding up into the wall with a small interior step, characteristic of bell-shaped bowls; footring always edged on the outside.
Base curving into the wall with small inner offset; outer-edged footring; from bell-shaped bowl forms.
Rounded transition into a steeper wall with small inner step; outer-edged footring.
Curved base-to-wall junction with small interior offset; tall edged footring of bell-shaped bowls.
Steeply rising rounded wall with small inner step; high outer-edged footring of glockenförmige bowls.
Footring edged both inside and outside (early forms fluted outside); smooth grooved floor arching up into the wall.
Footring with outer edge or groove; smooth, internally grooved rounded floor rising into the wall.
Footring with outer edge or groove; smooth round upward-curving floor merging into the wall.
Footring with outer edge or groove; smooth, grooved rounded floor of larger bowls rising steeply into the wall.
Low footring set on a broad resting surface; smooth grooved floor arching up into the wall.
Higher footring resting on a broad surface; smooth grooved rounded floor rising into the wall.
Footring with triangular cross-section (low version); smooth grooved floor curving into the wall.
Footring with triangular cross-section in a tall version; smooth grooved rounded floor rising steeply into the wall.
Foot-ring variant of cups (Forms 22-25): annular standring with obliquely rising wall, wall transition marked inside by a groove; tall/thicker ring profile.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): low annular standring, obliquely rising wall, inner wall transition grooved.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): standring with steeply oblique wall rising from foot, base modestly profiled.
Stepped foot-ring (inside and outside stepped/abgetreppt), oblique wall; characteristic of Padana cups (Subform 24.3).
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): low standring, flat base, obliquely rising wall.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): standring with grooved/facetted outer side, oblique wall, inner transition grooved.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): taller standring with steeply oblique wall, lens-thickened/rounded base.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): low broad standring, oblique wall, grooved inner transition.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): standring with oblique wall, flat to rounded base.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): standring with grooved outer face, oblique wall rising from foot.
Foot-ring variant (Forms 22-25): standring with steeply oblique wall, grooved inner transition, rounded base.
Low edged (gekantet) standring with flat base; wall sets on inside with a sharp kink and rises steeper than B 4.1-11. Typical of Form 23.
Low edged standring, flat base; sharply kinked steeply rising inner wall. Typical of Form 23.
Base variant of Forms 26-27: low broadly seated standring, mostly flat base, inner wall transition marked by groove/ridge; wall rises notably flatter than B 4.1-11.
Base variant of Forms 26-27: low broad standring, flat base, shallowly rising wall with grooved inner transition.
Base variant of Forms 26-27: low broad standring, edged outer face, flat base, shallowly rising wall.
Base variant of Forms 26-27: low broad standring, flat base, shallowly rising wall with grooved inner transition.

Hemispherical chalice with tall vertical rim; lip carries a small (sometimes rouletted) moulding with grooves above the relief zone. Sub-type R 10.1 has a broad convex moulding mid-way up the outer rim matched by a concave hollow on the interior.
Variant of the tall-rimmed hemispherical chalice where the convex moulding on the rim is narrower and only modifies the outer surface, leaving the interior unaffected.

Broad beaker or deep cup on a disk base with a curving body and a vertical rim ending in a grooved or everted lip; the rim is set off from the relief decoration outside by a double groove (occasionally relief extends to the lip).
Deep curving chalice on a pedestal foot with a hanging rim; outer rim face straight to slightly convex and decorated with one or more grooves, sometimes with rouletting.
Chalice with flaring body on a pedestal foot; outer rim face concave, framed by convex mouldings above and below, recalling plain Forms 17 and 21.
Deep curving chalice on a pedestal foot whose rim is reduced to a simple upright band set above a prominent quarter-round moulding.
Small, fairly thick-walled vessel of low capacity; both the ring foot and the wall splay outward, rim and base diameters roughly equal, but the interior tapers conically downward. Unstamped.
Knobbed lid with a plain, unprofiled smooth rim; the wall is straight, incurving or slightly bulged. Unstamped.
Knobbed lid whose edge ends in a rounded bead lip. Unstamped.
Knobbed lid with a split/grooved rim edge designed to improve seating on the vessel. Unstamped.
Deep cup with near-vertical to slightly curved wall, a thickened rolled rim and a band of close rouletting/notched decoration on the upper wall; possibly a modiolus.
Cup with curved wall and slightly inturned/thickened rim above moulded grooves; deeper variant (99.2.2) shows a carinated lower body with a rouletted band over a ring base.
Cup with a hooked/everted rim and a shallow curved wall carrying an upper rouletted band, sitting on a low rounded base.
Beaker/cup with an everted moulded rim, convex wall and a rouletted band low on the body above a flat base.

Chalice with deep curving body on a pedestal foot; heavy rim of near-triangular section, often with fine grooves and cordons outside, linked to the body by a quarter-round element set off below by a band of grooves; interior quarter-round separated from rim and body by offsets/grooves.
Chalice variant with deep curving body and pedestal foot, but a much slighter rim lacking external grooves; on the inside a small concave moulding sits above the quarter-round element.
Beaker with gently S-curved wall and a rounded transition; low standring foot, ungglazed interior wall.
Beaker with a curved (bowed) wall, low standring; banded surface ornament near the rim.
Cylindrical-walled beaker with an angular carination; underside of base may show concentric rings imitating metal vessels; banded decoration on wall.
origin: Italy and Gaul (production not closely localized)

description: Cylindrical beaker like 50.3 but with an everted or thickened rim; wall may carry barbotine ornament.
Strongly bulging globular beaker with a cyma (karnies) rim and scale-pattern decoration on the body.
Cup with tapering near-cylindrical body, flat base and a single vertical handle; rim profiled as in R 2.1.
Modiolus cup variant with the rim profiled as in R 2.2; tapering cylindrical body with vertical handle.
Modiolus cup with the rim simplified to a plain triangular section; tapering cylindrical body, single vertical handle and flat base.

Most common subtype: hemispherical bowl with horizontal rim (level or slightly dropped) set off from the wall by a groove or ridge, with an applied often grooved vertical edge-strip; ring foot, flat or slightly domed floor.
Wall flatter and more spreading; rim formation can be more strongly blurred, without barbotine decoration; domed floor.
Strongly curved profile with barbotine decoration also extending onto the wall; produced in Tardo-Italica ware.
Flat-floored dish with flaring wall and a vertical rim ledge; the steep rim is sharply offset from the wall by a distinct kink both inside and out, with a more strongly curved wall.
Flat-floored dish with flaring wall and vertical rim ledge; rim curved up and rounded inside, set off only by grooves, with a gently curving wall.
Cup version of the Form 48 dishes: flat base, flaring wall and vertical rim ledge; rim sharply offset from the wall by a distinct kink inside and outside.
Cup with flat base, flaring wall and vertical rim ledge; rim rounded and curved up, marked inside by grooves and sometimes club-like thickened.

Hemispherical relief-decorated chalice on a pedestal foot; profiled upright rim set apart from the relief zone by a short quarter-round moulding, with external mouldings echoing plain-ware forms and a generally smooth inner rim.

Pedestalled chalice with finely moulded concave upright rim (plain concave element framed by rouletted convex mouldings) directly above a truncated conical body carrying two relief zones divided by a rouletted convex moulding.
Pedestalled chalice with finely moulded concave upright rim above a hemispherical body bearing a single undivided relief zone; distinguished from R7.1 by the angle where the body meets the rim.

Chalice with a narrow hanging rim whose outer face carries rouletting, separated from the relief-decorated lower body by a tall, fairly straight plain zone; a roulette-decorated convex moulding sits just above the relief band. Rim profile resembles Form R 2.1.

Variant chalice in which the external profile of the hanging rim is sharply angular, with the inner mouldings correspondingly distorted; tall plain zone above the relief decoration, with rouletted rim and convex moulding as on R 4.1.

Carinated bowl with straight flaring wall, sloping floor and a small foot. A large convex moulding sits below the rim with a small ridge beneath it, mirrored inside by two grooves. Type A bears rouletted decoration (two or three lines on the moulding under the rim, single or sometimes double lines above and below the carination, often deeply impressed into a continuous groove); Type B is plain with a more flaring wall. Early Type A examples are thin-fabricked with a steeply rising wall and fine rouletting. Type A D. c. 12.5–23; Type B generally larger, D. c. 19–27. One of the commonest early shapes alongside Form 9.
Type A: relatively small, shallow flanged bowl with a plain rim; fabric tends to be poor with a thin dull slip; floor sometimes carries a group of fine scratch-like grooves.

Type B: larger and deeper flanged bowl with a more strongly projecting flange and an internal rim-roll (sometimes like a flat raised fillet); poor fabric with thin dull slip, and the upper exterior is often blackened by uneven firing.

Undecorated bowl with straight sloping or vertical wall, sloping floor and a small low foot, more or less carinated. Three variants: A is fairly deep with an outward-sloping wall curving into the floor (plain version of Form 9A); B is more open with a vertical wall; C is shallow and open with a low inward-sloping wall (treated as a dish, cf. Form 18). Common, normal diameter c. 16–20.
Carinated bowl resembling Form 14, with a thick rim bevelled along the top. Fairly deep body with a vertical, slightly convex wall and thick fabric; a debased version of Form 14.
Small dish related to Form 14, with a low flaring wall, sloping floor and a small low foot; slightly carinated and undecorated. Comparable to shallower versions of Form 9B.
Shallow bowl with flaring wall and low foot, transitional 14/17 profile.

id: African Red Slip Ware Form 17B var
description: Shallow dish, low flaring wall and small foot (Form 17 B variant).

Shallow dish with a broad, nearly flat floor, a low steep wall and a low small-diameter foot; thick bright slip; fairly large. Variants have very low or low curved rims, one in finer splintery fabric transitional toward later forms.
Mould-made rectangular dish, possibly with scalloped ends; flat floor on a low foot, low wall, and a wide flat rim carrying relief decoration (fish, baskets, fisherman with beaded borders).
Flat-based dish with a curved wall; a small groove runs inside just below the rim, with grooves on the floor and a slight offset at the wall-floor junction. Rare.

Wide-based dish with wall set at a slight angle externally; a groove runs inside just below the rim, and the floor bears two sets of paired grooves. Slip typically thin and matt with a slightly pimply surface; grooves narrow and scratchy in appearance. Normal diameter c. 20–28, occasionally larger.

Form evolving from a deep rounded bowl toward a shallower carinated profile, the latest examples resembling dishes close to Form 16. Earlier Type A pieces have a rounded rim with a convex moulding bearing rouletting; later simplified to two grooves enclosing a rouletted flat band. Some small shallow variants carry an extra rouletted line low on the body.

Large carinated bowl with a steep sloping wall and a heavy knobbed rim formed of a large external moulding with a subsidiary flat fillet beneath; a small lip usually at the inner edge. Curved floor on a small foot, with a small external ledge and internal inset at the wall/floor junction. Type A has rouletting on the lower rim-moulding and below the carination; Type B is undecorated.
Casserole with rounded body, short concave neck and a low vertical rim; small low foot like the Form 2 series. Rim has rouletting; slipped on the exterior only.
Lid matching Form 21; simple conical shape with a small knob. Some have two lines of fine rouletting with a small groove at the rim, others are plain. Slip on top only.

Common dish form developing from a small Type A to larger Type B versions; flaring walls (sometimes very flaring), some with a raised fillet inside the rim, and grooves on the floor (number varies, sometimes absent).
Variant with a broad rim resembling Form 2 but without the groove, and a relatively deep body; decorated with four well-executed barbotine leaves.
Narrow flattened rim with a groove near its inner edge; junction of wall and floor with a small offset above the foot. Medium-sized form with thick bright slip.

Shallow dish with a curved floor, broad convex rim, and a small low foot; the deeper counterpart of Form 2. Rim often carries barbotine leaf decoration. Three variants: Type A has a broad rim with a groove on the inner edge and barbotine leaves; Type B has barbotine decoration but no groove and a usually narrower rim; Type C is like B but plain. Mostly medium-sized (D. c. 16-21), with small versions (D. c. 10-11) and occasional large pieces (D. 25+).

Dish with a flaring wall carrying mouldings at top and bottom and an internal moulding where the wall meets the floor; small foot and sloping floor as on Form 3, with a groove on the inner face of the rim. Type A has a rouletted circle on the floor (sometimes rouletting on the wall/floor moulding, occasionally a small central stamp); Type B lacks rouletting and is broader and shallower. Related to Gaulish samian Dragendorff 15/17.

Dish closely copying the Italian terra sigillata Dragendorff 18 shape: flat floor, straight steep wall with a slight rolled rim, square-cut foot; decorated with grooves on the floor, a slight offset where floor meets wall, and a groove inside the rim. Very rare.

Curved, more or less hemispherical to conical bowl on a small low foot; broad convex rim with a groove on its inner edge, decorated with a string of barbotine leaves (four to six). A deeper variant has a narrow ungrooved rim.

Dish with a sloping, slightly offset wall and a small rim-roll; floor and foot like Form 4, often with a groove halfway up the wall. Related to Drag. 18. Type A: rouletted circle on floor, groove inside rim, flaring slightly concave wall, sometimes planta pedis stamp. Type B: rouletted circle, groove on top of rim, steeper wall. Type C: simplified, no rouletting or rim groove, heavier rolled rim, sometimes external wall groove.

Dish form (concluding discussion); some examples (nos. 13-15) have a single groove on the floor rather than rouletting, forming a transition. Marked carination (Lamboglia 23b) and small carinated bowls (Type C) are the latest in the series. Often found with a poor dull slip.

Bowl with a steep wall curving into a sloping floor, a thickened or rolled rim, and a low foot. Exterior carries two or three zones of rouletting separated by a groove midway up the wall. Type A has two grooves on the interior wall with rather fine rouletting and is sometimes thin-walled and finely made; Type B has a plain interior with coarser rouletting, a heavier rolled rim and a more angular body. Diameter roughly 16-23 cm.

Casserole with nearly vertical wall and rim divided by a concave moulding; floor slightly concave, sometimes with fine grooving underneath. Occasionally has three stub feet. Rim concave inside with a marked ledge below; slip applied only on exterior.

Shallow conical flanged lid with a small knob and a broad flat rim ending in a small vertical flange below. A raised fillet sits above the rim, usually with a small ridge at the junction; rouletting normally on rim and/or body. Slip on the upper surface only, extending to the rim edge. Serves as the lid for Form 19.
Shallow open dish/casserole with flaring wall and rounded base, plain rim.
Deeper flaring casserole with curved wall rising to a simple rim and rounded/footed base; some rouletting on lower wall.
Large carinated bowl like Form 10 but with a slightly thickened rim bearing a groove or ledge on top; below the rim a frilled, finger-impressed applied cordon. Diameter about 27-35 cm.
Small bowl with incurving wall, sloping floor and a rim carrying a small external flange; some examples have rouletting (one line on the flange edge, three on the wall); presumed small foot.

Small dish related to Form 6 but with a flat rim carrying small mouldings on its outer and inner edges, with stamped ornament between them; a groove runs around the edge of the floor and a rouletted circle around the centre. Thin fabric with fine glossy slip.
Curved-wall bowl with rouletted decorative bands on the interior wall and a low ring foot.
Larger deep bowl with curved wall, grooved rim and low foot ring.

Small bowl with curved wall, plain rim and a low foot; diameter c. 10-13 cm. Two variants: A is shallower with a small-diameter foot and walls either slightly flaring or incurved (possibly derived from Form 14); B is more hemispherical with the foot set wider out (foot-to-rim diameter ratio c. 3:5).

Plate with a broad floor rising slightly at the edge to a wide flat rim; low foot of medium diameter. Rim has low mouldings at inner and outer edges with a series of appliqué motifs (fishes, rosettes, animals, trees, lozenges, flowers) between them; grooves on the floor, sometimes a central appliqué. Medium to large; uncommon.

Dish with broad flat floor, low curved wall and low foot of small diameter. Short flattened rim sometimes grooved near the inner edge; wall set off from the floor by a small external flange with a matching internal inset. Possible development of Form 4B.
Large dish with flat floor carried on a small foot at its outer edge, low curving wall and knobbed rim, with an offset above the foot. Thick bright slip showing smoothing marks; rather thick fabric.
Small bowl with a slightly everted, thickened rim and curving wall.
Shallow dish/bowl with a thin incurved rim and low flaring wall.

Dish with broad flat rim, shallow curved body with a faint external carination matched by an interior groove, small low foot; rim plain except a groove at the lip. Type A has a rouletted circle on the floor. Diameters c. 19-22, with a smaller version c. 11-12.

Same dish form as 6A (broad flat rim, shallow curved slightly carinated body, low foot, lip groove) but with a plain undecorated floor; some examples show a groove around the centre of the floor, possibly transitional from Type A.
Deeper variant of the small type, comparable to bowls of Form 2, with a more pronounced carination. Diameter c. 12, height c. 3-4. Uncommon.

Shallow dish with a fairly curved wall, low flat foot and sagging floor; sometimes two grooves on the floor. Slip varies, either resembling Form 27 or thick and bright like third-century dishes; two distinct fabrics seem present. Diameter roughly 20-34 cm.
Shallow flaring dish with a low foot; profile with grooved interior near rim.
Shallow flaring dish with a low foot.

A distinct intermediate type between Form 27 and Form 31, similar in shape to the shallow curved dish but with an inward-curving rim; thick slip with smoothing marks. One related fragment has a small groove inside the rim.

Bowl with a tall, slightly bulging vertical wall and flat rim; shallow floor on a small foot recalling second-century types; two grooves run along the wall above the carination. Uncommon, diameter c. 14-17 cm.

Small bowl with vertical wall, flat floor and tiny foot; a small double moulding at the rim with an interior groove, plus further small mouldings beneath the vessel. Mould-made relief decoration on the wall (lion and panther flanking a stylized tree, mask and thyrsos); modelled on metalware prototypes. One known example, diameter 7.8 cm.
Shallow bowl/dish with curving wall, flat base and a plain rim bevelled on the inner side; a groove runs inside just below the rim and appliqué motifs decorate the floor.
Shallow bowl akin to Form 39 but with a wide out-turned rim and a very small foot; groove on the interior at the rim/body junction and appliqué decoration around the floor.

Large dish with a wide flat floor, low sloping wall and broad flat sloping rim; small foot set under the outer floor. The rim broadens at each end into a flat grip-handle with a symmetrically fretted edge. Plain apart from a few grooves on rim and floor, with thin glossy slip covering the surface.

Small hemispherical bowl with broad, slightly convex flaring rim and small low foot; sometimes a groove at the lip. A variant has a horizontal rim with two grooves at the lip and a broad raised fillet down the middle. Common in Tunisia, uncommon elsewhere.

Open dish/plate with slip covering interior and rim only, base merely smoothed and sometimes showing faint brush- or twig-marks; floor may carry pairs of fine grooves or a lathe-mark. Type B variants show a quarter-round or developing inset foot. Decorated variants bear appliqué motifs on the rim — alternating animals and trees, or animals and a venator with shrubs and birds. A variant type has a low chamfered vertical wall surmounted by a broad oblique flat rim with a groove at the lip.

id: African Red Slip Ware Type A
description: Large flat dishes/plates (D. c. 32-50 cm) with low or knobbed/high foot and grooved borders (typically triple grooves near the rim). Central floor bears stamped relief decoration: jewelled crosses, cross-monograms, standing figures with spears or in orans pose, birds, rosettes, lambs, and Christian scenes. A group of related large stamped-decoration dishes.
cross_refs: De Rossi, Bull. di arch. crist. 2 ser. iv (1873) 125

id: African Red Slip Ware Type B
description: Slightly carinated open form with straight flaring wall and a sagging base; diameters c. 19 cm. Undecorated variant of the appliqué series.

Open dish like Form 42 but with a broad rim shaped into a polygonal (roughly eight-sided) outline with slightly concave edges; fine fabric akin to Forms 52-53/56. Grooves at the lip following the scalloping and a groove over the small angular foot. Appliqué motifs (animals, trees with birds, panthers) set at the angles where rim sides meet.

Large circular dish, like Form 54 but round, with applied (appliqué) figural decoration on the rim and one to three grooves at the lip; thick-walled with thick lustrous slip. Appliqué motifs include standing figures, a sailing ship with heads, and biblical scenes (Abraham's Sacrifice, Daniel in the lions' den). Rare.

Small bowl with steep straight wall, broad flat rim, and small low foot; successor to Form 44. Fairly thin-walled, fine slightly granular ware with thin matt slip inside and over the rim. Surfaces well-smoothed except underside of rim. Rim rises slightly with plain or slightly hooked, bevelled and grooved lip; low square-cut foot. Groove at rim lip and another on floor. Type A: undecorated with plain lip. Type B: appliqué decoration on rim (usually three or four well-spaced small motifs such as animals, masks, leaves, capitals).

Very large dish in two variants. Type A carries moulded relief decoration on the floor: a central rectangular relief panel framed by grooves, encircled by a double rouletted band, with separate applied motifs between grooved borders on the outer floor and another double rouletted band near the rim; the foot bears a broad double rouletted band between grooves with a projecting moulding above. Type B has stamped or plain floors with varied rouletting and grooves on the foot, sometimes with a moulding. Relief scenes include arena/venatores and animal-combat motifs (lions, boar).

Open dish/bowl with flat floor, slightly curved sloping wall and flat rim, with a small foot under the outer floor; appliqué decoration. Broader, shallower relative of Form 52. Type A has a broad flat circular rim with appliqués (single example); Type B has a narrower rim that widens at each end into grip-handles with fretted edge (smaller than Form 42), with appliqués on handles and rim.

Dish with flat base, curved flaring wall and a flat, slightly drooping rim. Fine-grained fabric with thin smooth slip inside and on the upper exterior. Base of fairly small diameter, with a slight moulding at the edge or meeting the wall at a slight angle; interior floor edge rises above the base of the wall. One or two grooves on the rim and on the floor.
Small deep bowl with straight flaring wall, flat floor and broad flat rim; thin flaring foot of medium height. Thin fabric with fine glossy slip overall. Rare.

Plate with broad flat floor from which a convex everted rim rises, sometimes with a slight wall; tiny bevelled foot under the outer floor edge. Thin, hard, pure ware with sharp breaks; carefully smoothed surfaces with fine close-set turning marks outside near the base; usually one small groove at the lip. A finer version of Form 33. Type A has a roughly horizontal rim with bright glossy slip over the whole vessel; Type B has an obliquely flaring rim with a slight wall and thin smooth slip.

Plate similar to Form 48 but with a low curved wall terminating in a sharply incurved rim; fine fabric like Form 50 with closely spaced fine turning-marks on the wall exterior; diameter range about 23-40 cm. A variant is more open without the incurved rim, thicker ware, with a small ledge-foot and two circles at the center of the floor.

Deep bowl resembling Form 34 but taller with a more upright wall and a plain moulded rim; thin walls of fairly fine fabric bear sparse appliqué figures on the wall. A variant is shallower with an inward-sloping wall and everted rim.

Bowl with convex wall topped by a short concave neck and an upright moulded rim; shallow curved floor on a small foot. Small mouldings at the carination and underside; wall decorated with appliqué motifs separated by vertical palmette dividers, including mythological scenes.

Deep bowl with rounded body slightly incurved beneath the rim, with a broad flat rim; foot probably as on preceding forms. Rim carries small mouldings at the lip and inner edge, with a band of applied motifs between them.

Large flat dish that evolves over a long sequence: earliest pieces have sharply incurved rims (recalling Form 49) with an almost horizontal chamfer and thinner, better-finished fabric; the standard Type A has a less incurved rim chamfered at roughly 45 degrees, tending toward a more vertical rim with sloping chamfer and slight basal overhang. One development gives a steep sloping wall with tall upright rim marked off inside and out; another (Type B) has shallower, longer walls at the expense of the floor with a hooked rim and thick bright slip. Crude transitional pieces have more open form but less developed rims and broad floors. Specimens show projecting/triangular rims, reduced floors, two grooves under floor, and stamped decoration (toothed rings, quadruple circles).
Shallow open bowl with rounded lower wall and simple incurved rim; rouletted/notched decoration on the upper exterior wall.
Shallow open bowl with curving wall and plain rim; faint grooved/dashed interior banding.
Shallow bowl with sinuous wall and slightly thickened rim; one full profile and a separate rim sherd shown.
Large bowl similar to Form 45 but with a broad curving rim; fabric like later Form 45 with a thickish, dull slip; floor sometimes with fine grooves. Uncommon.
Flat shallow dish with low flaring wall and simple rim; near-flat floor.
Flat shallow dish with short flaring wall and flat floor; thin interior grooving.

Dish with broad flat floor, sloping wall and short flat rim; small foot of relatively large diameter. Slight inset inside at wall/floor junction; outside the wall meets the bottom at an angle just beyond the foot line. Occasional grooves on floor and underside. Thick coarse fabric with thick bright slip.

Plate; a shallower version of Form 32 with variable fabric. Medium to large size, often with grooves on floor; some examples with pronounced or very low walls, slip ranging from dull to thick and bright.

Large, generally thin-walled bowl with a shallow curving body and a broad flat rim rising obliquely; flat base with a shallow triangular foot at the edge marked by a slight inset. Three variants: A with bands of fine rouletting on rim and floor plus fine grooving at the lip; B plain with grooves on rim and floor; C like B but with the rim drooping to a slightly hooked edge. Diameter range c. 21-40 cm.
Large flaring dish with thickened, grooved flat-topped rim and low foot.

Large flat-based dish with a curved wall and a short flat rim; lower wall serves as resting surface, with a broad slightly hollowed base set off by a small inset or tiny foot and a matching interior offset/groove at the floor edge. Usually grooves on rim and floor; floor often sags. Type A: finer hard-fired brownish to maroon-red clay, lustrous slip overall, sometimes twig-marks underneath, sharp-cut rims and steep walls; Type B: coarser granular orange-red clay, semi-lustrous/matt slip inside and on upper exterior only, shallower with sloping walls and downturned rims.
Flaring dish with thickened grooved rim and low foot.

Derivative of Form 32 with a flat base and no separate foot; wall flares and meets the floor at an angle. Grooves on the floor (one near edge, two near centre on some pieces) and none on the rim. Slip applied only to the interior and upper exterior rather than the whole surface. Two main fabrics: Type A related to Form 45, Type B in the later stamped-ware fabric with mostly unslipped exterior; transitional toward the stamped wares but never itself stamped.

Relief (appliqué) decorated bowl, Type A, occurring in two shape variants: a canonical version with a regular grooving scheme, and a shallower, more open variant with the rim-grooves (usually three) set near the lip and either a single wide floor-groove or none. Appliqué motifs are related in subject and generally form a single composition covering the interior; canonical pieces show animal and venatio scenes in a band plus figured scenes (e.g. Mithras cycle), while the variant carries allegorical and Judaeo-Christian themes in a single field. Closely related in decoration to Form 56 and Form 52B.
Flaring shallow dish with thin curved walls rising from a flat floor.
Flaring dish, transitional variant, curved walls from flat floor with rim hatching shown.
Deep flaring dish with sweeping curved wall to flat floor.
Large bowl with curved wall, broad flat rim and small foot; rouletting on rim and floor with appliqué decoration around the interior (e.g. venatio motifs).

Shallow plate, essentially a low version of Form 45 with the characteristic base; rim nearly horizontal and only slightly raised above the floor; thin fabric, fine rather dark mottled slip, with a groove at the lip and several grooves on the floor.

Large dish, direct successor of Form 63; examples range from shallower open forms with sagging floor and thick walls to small deep variants. Floor decoration in a narrow band between sets of fine grooves, including chevrons forming a star-pattern and fringed circles, with stamped Style A(iii) ornament. A shallow flaring-walled variant (classed Form 50B/64) has a flat base with inset ridge at the floor edge, granular fabric with lustrous slip, undecorated.

Flat-based dish resembling Form 59B but with a plain flat rim bearing a groove at the lip; similar fabric and decoration. Wide floor with triple grooves bearing rows of small incuse rosettes, or palms and circles. Rare.

Large plate with a broad flattened rim rising obliquely to a heavy hooked lip, the rim offset from the floor by a low straight wall; outside of rim bevelled, top flat with grooves at the lip and inner edge, and a broad flat floor.

Fairly large dish with flat base, low curved wall and broad flat rim rising gently to a knobbed rim; a coarser version of Form 75. Granular ware similar to Form 67 with thin dull slip inside and over the rim and rather pimply surfaces. Base like Form 67 with low base-moulding and groove near the edge; sometimes a pair of grooves on the rim, and a central stamp may occur.

Large plate with a shallow curving floor, small angular foot and thickened rim that continues the line of the floor; rim thickened below with a convex outer face and flat bevelled underside, with grooves/ridges at the rim and around the floor.

Small bowl with steep wall, low foot and broad flat rim. Square-cut rim with a hanging, externally bevelled lip and two grooves running along the middle of the rim. Plain floor; brownish fabric slipped all over, occasionally with twig-marks beneath the base. Variants show double rouletted or roughly rouletted bands on the rim.

Small bowl with wheelmarks; slightly hooked lip bearing groups of small triangular notches along the upper edge, and one or more grooves on the floor. Type A: rim of two flat bands divided by a small ridge (inner narrow/horizontal, outer broader/sloping up). Type B: rim with two flat bands flanking a convex band with small ridges. D. 9-16.
Small bowl with plain rounded body and flat base; broad horizontal rim that is flat or slightly downturned. Coarse granular fabric with thick bright slip inside and over the rim.
Dish with carinated wall and flat base; rim has a small external flange. Lower wall meets the base at a very shallow angle and bears one or more grooves. Granular fabric with bright slip.
Deep bowl with curved flaring wall and simple rim; multiple grooved lines on the interior wall.
Deep bowl with steep flaring wall and plain rim, low base.
